title: Women's Rights
objective: After this level you can explain the legal rights Egyptian women had.
summary: Egyptian women could own and sell property, make contracts and go to court in their own name, as Naunakhte’s will shows. But equal in law was not equal in life.

cards.headline: An Egyptian mother cut some of her children out of her will. The law let her.
cards.body: Her name was Naunakhte, and her will survives on papyrus. It shows something unusual for the ancient world: a woman with legal rights of her own.

cards.headline: Equal on paper
cards.body: From the Old Kingdom on, an Egyptian woman’s formal legal status was nearly identical to a man’s, married or not. She could buy, own and sell property in her own name, make contracts, take someone to court or be sued, and act as a witness. She didn’t need a man to represent her. Britannica puts it a notch lower: her status was “only marginally inferior” to a man’s. Either way, that was rare in the ancient world.

cards.headline: Naunakhte’s will
cards.body: Naunakhte lived in Deir el-Medina, the tomb builders’ village you’ll visit in Level 59. In old age she set out which of her children would inherit from her, and left out the ones who hadn’t cared for her or supported her. Her property was hers to divide, completely separate from her husband’s. Look after your mother: in Egypt, it could be a legal matter.

cards.headline: Equal in law, not in life
cards.body: Don’t picture equality, though. Socially, men and women were not equal. Women seldom held paid public posts, so they usually earned less and depended on family, which could leave them worse off if a marriage ended. Even though the law allowed it, women rarely served as witnesses to legal documents. Egyptian women had rights on paper that most ancient women never had. Daily life still ran on men’s terms.
cards.callout: Legal rights: nearly equal. Daily life: not equal.

mascot.line: Don’t mix these up: equal in law is not the same as equal in life.

cards.headline: Women’s rights: weighed

questions.prompt: Which of these could an Egyptian woman legally do in her own name?

options.label: Nothing without her husband’s signature
options.rationale: She didn’t need a man to represent her.

options.label: Own property and bring a case to court
Only inherit from her father
options.rationale: She could buy, own and sell property herself.

options.label: Only own clothes and jewelry
options.rationale: She could own and sell property of all kinds.

questions.explanation: Women could own, buy and sell property, make contracts, go to court and act as witnesses in their own name.

questions.prompt: Why did Naunakhte leave some of her children out of her will?

options.label: They had moved away from Egypt
options.rationale: Her reason was about care, not distance.

options.label: The law barred sons from inheriting
options.rationale: Egyptian law let her choose her heirs.

options.label: They hadn’t cared for or supported her in old age
Her husband ordered her to
options.rationale: Her property was separate from his.

questions.explanation: She excluded the children who hadn’t cared for or supported her, and the property was hers to divide.

questions.prompt: From Level 54: girls mostly learned home life from their mothers. How does that fit Egyptian women’s working lives?

options.label: Women held most government offices
options.rationale: Women seldom held paid public posts.

Women were banned from owning property
options.rationale: They could own and sell property.

options.label: Women trained as scribes more often than men
options.rationale: Schooling was rare, and mostly for elite boys.

questions.explanation: Raised for home life, few women held paid public posts, so they usually earned less and depended on family.
